title: Miketz: weeping in private (Genesis 43:30–31)
hook: Joseph leaves to cry, washes his face, and comes back in

segments.voice: Yesterday, the brothers saying out loud, we are verily guilty. Your line was guilt remembers. This week: God going down into Egypt, a sad face noticed, two years ending in a day, not in me, dreams in the dark, and guilt. Today, Joseph's tears. Day two hundred ten.

You're at work, or at a wedding, or a kid's recital, and something hits you. A memory, a face, a piece of news. Your throat closes. And you say, excuse me, one second, and walk fast down the hallway to the bathroom, and lock the door. The brothers have come back to Egypt, and this time they've brought the youngest, Benjamin. Joseph's only full brother, the other son of Rachel. The last time Joseph saw him, Benjamin was just a boy. Today: weeping in private.
screen: `EXCUSE ME, ONE SECOND.` → `BENJAMIN COMES TO EGYPT.` → `THE OTHER SON OF RACHEL.`

segments.voice: Joseph asks them about their father: is the old man well? Is he still alive? Then he lifts his eyes and sees Benjamin, his mother's son. Is this your youngest brother, the one you told me about? And he says to him: God be gracious to you, my son. And then, the Torah says, Joseph hurried. His compassion for his brother welled up, the Hebrew says, it grew warm inside him, and he looked for a place to cry. "And he entered into his chamber, and wept there." Then, three short actions. "And he washed his face." He came out. And he held himself back, the Hebrew word is vayit'apak, he restrained himself, and said: serve the meal. Stop and look at that sequence. He doesn't pretend nothing happened. He lets himself cry, fully, alone. And then he washes his face and walks back into the room, because the room still needs him. There's a plan in motion, and a family that isn't ready to know who he is yet. Joseph cries a lot in Genesis. Readers count about seven times: when the brothers confess, here, when he finally reveals himself, when he falls on Benjamin's neck, when he sees his father, when his father dies, and when his brothers ask forgiveness. The most powerful man in Egypt is also the one who cries most in the book. Jewish tradition has never treated tears as weakness. The Talmud even says that when all the gates of prayer are locked, the gates of tears are not. But there's also a time to wash your face. Both are part of it.
screen: `GOD BE GRACIOUS TO YOU, MY SON.` · `HE WEPT IN HIS CHAMBER.` · `HE WASHED HIS FACE, AND CAME OUT.` · `THE GATES OF TEARS ARE NOT LOCKED.` · then, large: `WASH YOUR FACE, GO BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let yourself cry when you need to. Settle, and breathe. Is there something you've been holding back? A grief, a relief, a joy too big for the room. You don't have to force tears. Just give whatever is there some space, the way Joseph found a room. If tears come, let them. Then, when you're ready, picture washing your face with cool water, and stepping back into your day. The bell holds the time.
Miketz. At the end: the portion where Joseph sees Benjamin, weeps alone in his room, washes his face, and comes back in.
Your line: wash your face, go back. Today, if something moves you, give it a real moment, even behind a closed door, and then return. Day two hundred ten.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition makes room for tears in prayer, especially on the High Holy Days, and teaches that the gates of tears are never locked; Joseph's weeping is read each winter in Miketz and Vayigash.
